questions.q: What is the specific irony Asimov highlights when he compares the "crystal ball" to "television sets of today"?
questions.a: The irony is that the crystal ball — a magical object requiring supernatural power to see distant events — has been surpassed in function by television, a mundane technological device that achieves the same result through electromagnetic waves, making the "magic" obsolete and the "miracle" ordinary. A wrong answer (e.g., "both show pictures") reveals the student sees only surface similarity, missing the irony that science has democratized what magic reserved for the chosen few.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Asimov calls the ancient gods "whimsical and unpredictable" and how this description serves his larger argument about the universe of science fiction.
questions.a: Asimov describes gods as whimsical because natural phenomena (storms, earthquakes) seem random and senseless without scientific laws; this serves his argument by contrasting the prescientific universe — where outcomes depend on divine mood — with the science fiction universe — where outcomes follow knowable, controllable laws, making science fiction a more reliable framework for imagining the future. A wrong answer (e.g., "gods were mean") shows the student misses the structural contrast Asimov builds between capricious divine will and impersonal natural law.

questions.q: In Section II, Asimov writes: "A story may involve... gas gun and sphere in an atmosphere enclosed on a space station under zero gravity. It is still a sports story... but it is science fiction also." Identify the symbolic function of the "gas gun and sphere" in this passage.
questions.a: The "gas gun and sphere" symbolize how science fiction transplants familiar human activities (sports) into alien settings without changing their essential nature — the game remains a game, but the equipment symbolizes adapted physics. The student must recognize that the object stands for the principle: content (sport) stays constant while background (physics) changes. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's just a futuristic hockey stick") treats it as mere props, missing its symbolic role in proving Asimov's thesis about genre definition.

questions.q: Analyze how Asimov's reference to John Campbell's "failure of nerve" regarding science fiction mysteries creates dramatic irony for the reader who knows Asimov's own novels (The Caves of Steel, The Naked Sun).
questions.a: The dramatic irony arises because Asimov the essayist cites Campbell's authoritative claim that SF mysteries are impossible, while Asimov the novelist has already written successful ones — the reader who knows this sees the "failure of nerve" as ironically premature. The student must connect the essay's rhetorical strategy (quoting an expert to then disprove him) with external textual knowledge. A wrong answer (e.g., "Campbell was wrong") states the outcome but misses the irony's structural function: it validates Asimov's credibility and the genre's flexibility.

questions.q: Evaluate whether Asimov's comparison of faith in ancient magical formulas to modern faith in "economists, sociologists, and meteorologists" is a fair analogy or a false equivalence. Justify with evidence from the text.
questions.a: It is a deliberate satirical analogy, not a false equivalence: Asimov explicitly signals it with "We needn't sneer" and parallels the unfalsifiability of both systems (failed formulas blame offenders; failed predictions blame model complexity). The irony deepens because science claims falsifiability, yet these fields often evade it — mirroring the priestly defense of magic. A weak evaluation (e.g., "it's funny but unfair") misses that Asimov uses the analogy to undermine the superiority complex of "scientific" modernity, reinforcing his theme that emotional needs persist across epistemic shifts.

questions.q: Create a new symbolic object for a 22nd-century science fiction story that functions like Asimov's "seven-league boots" — representing a current human desire through a futuristic device. Explain the desire it symbolizes and the irony its future ubiquity would create.
questions.a: Example: "Neural-link contact lenses" that project any environment onto the retina — symbolizing the desire for instant escape from physical limitation. Irony: once universal, they make "real" travel a luxury for the poor, reversing today's status markers. A strong answer invents a plausible device, names the timeless desire (escape, omnipotence, connection), and projects the ironic social inversion. A poor answer (e.g., "a teleporter") merely names a trope without analyzing its symbolic desire or ironic consequence.
